headline_seed: Cornell students hold sit-in over alleged 2024 fraternity assault - NBC News

consensus_facts: A former Cornell University student known as Jane Doe alleges she was sexually assaulted by members of the Chi Phi fraternity at a fraternity house in October 2024.
Jane Doe recently filed a civil lawsuit against Cornell University and seven then-Chi Phi fraternity members.
Cornell conducted an internal investigation; two students were expelled and two were suspended, with additional lesser sanctions for others.
No criminal charges were brought against the accused at the time of the original 2024 probe.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James to serve as special prosecutor/oversee the case (CBS dates the executive order Oct. 1; NBC says James replaced DA Van Houten the prior week).
Cornell students staged a seven-hour sit-in on Oct. 7, 2026, in solidarity with Jane Doe (NBC and CNN); NBC reports roughly 80 students gathered at the Toni Morrison dining hall.

Cornell faculty introduced/are reviewing a resolution calling for a no-confidence vote in the university administration over its handling of the case (NBC; CNN reports it will be reviewed for the Oct. 14 Faculty Senate agenda).

Cornell brought in a former top U.S. Justice Department official — identified by ABC as former Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates — to lead an independent review of the university's handling of the allegations.
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten declined to charge the accused and has been criticized for that decision; the DA and university defended their original 2024 probes.
The alleged assault is described as having occurred over multiple hours during the night of Oct. 19-20, 2024, with Jane Doe alleging she was given ketamine (NBC and CBS).

positions.NBC News: Gov. Hochul 'effectively replaced' DA Van Houten as lead investigator 'last week,' appointing AG Letitia James to oversee the case.
positions.CBS News: Hochul signed an executive order on Oct. 1 appointing James as special prosecutor to investigate and, if warranted, prosecute.
The Tompkins County DA's Office confirmed on Sept. 28 it was reopening the criminal investigation amid community pressure.
positions.ABC News: A special prosecutor is opening a criminal investigation; characterizes two investigations as underway (criminal charges + university handling).
positions.NBC News: Frames it as James being appointed to oversee the case after criticism of Van Houten for declining to charge.

disagreements.topic: Nature of sanctions against accused students

positions.CBS News: Attorney Giuffra says two were expelled and five received lesser sanctions including suspensions, workshops and writing essays; Cornell disputes that any were offered essays as a sole consequence, and President Kotlikoff said two were expelled, two suspended, one had graduated, and two were found not responsible.

The DA said Jane Doe's November 2024 sworn statement differed from what she alleges in the civil lawsuit; her attorney says investigators never followed up. Transcript shows she distinguished initial consensual-leaning activity from later events she described as rape.
positions.ABC News: Reports campus police questioned fraternity members on how they knew the sex was 'consensual'; cites Jane Doe's panel testimony calling it being 'prostituted' and 'held up like bait.'

positions.CNN: Leads with Jane Doe receiving death threats, a swatting incident, and doxxing; attorney Giuffra says 'the temperature needs to be brought down.'
positions.NBC News: Does not mention threats against Jane Doe; focuses on the sit-in and faculty no-confidence resolution.
positions.ABC News: Does not mention threats; focuses on police interview videos and the independent review.
positions.CBS News: Does not mention threats; focuses on the lawsuit, investigation reopening, and interview transcript.

framing_analysis.Reuters: Headline-only in dossier. Frames the story as institutional accountability: 'Pressure mounting on Cornell administration, president over handling of alleged gang rape.' Emphasis is on the administration and president as the subject of scrutiny. No body text available to corroborate.
framing_analysis.NBC News (Article 2): Headline-only in dossier ('In solidarity with Jane Doe, Cornell students hold 7-hour sit-in'). Frames around student solidarity and the symbolic 7-hour duration.
framing_analysis.The New York Times: Headline-only in dossier. Uniquely frames the Cornell case as a national/political data point: 'Cornell Case Highlights Drop in Resolved Sexual Assault Cases Under Trump.' Ties a campus case to federal Title IX/enforcement trends under the Trump administration — a framing no other outlet in the dossier adopts. No body text to corroborate.
framing_analysis.NBC News (Article 4): Full body text. Leads with the student protest and the symbolic framing ('Seven hours for the seven hours she endured'). Emphasizes campus mood, the faculty no-confidence resolution, and the roster of progressive student groups organizing the sit-in (Black Students United, NAACP, Planned Parenthood Generation Action, ACLU chapter). Notes three accused men denied allegations through attorneys. Buries the evidentiary details of the assault. Frames James's involvement as welcomed by both Cornell and the DA.
framing_analysis.ABC News: Full body text. Leads with newly obtained police interview videos showing fraternity members telling Cornell police the encounter was 'consensual' and the officer pressing them on how they could know. Emphasizes investigative/evidentiary detail and Jane Doe's panel testimony ('prostituted,' 'held up like bait'). Reports Cornell expelled two and suspended two, and tapped Sally Yates for an independent review. Framing centers on scrutiny of the original police handling.
framing_analysis.CBS News: Full body text. Most document-driven account. Leads with the emerging case details and lawsuit, then lays out competing claims: the DA's statement that Doe's 2024 sworn statement differed from the civil suit, the attorney's claim investigators never followed up, and Cornell's point-by-point rebuttal on sanctions. Uniquely quotes the campus police interview transcript at length, including Doe distinguishing initial activity ('pretty OK with all of this') from later events ('I can say with 100% confidence I was raped'). Presents multiple sides' factual disputes side by side.
framing_analysis.CNN: Full body text. Leads with Jane Doe receiving death threats, a swatting incident, and doxxing — the harassment-and-backlash angle other outlets omit. Also covers the sit-in, the faculty no-confidence vote path (Oct. 14), a faculty member (Ariana Kim) calling for President Kotlikoff's resignation, two accused students still enrolled, and the Ithaca mayor seeking a moratorium on student/Greek-life gatherings. Broadest frame: a 'nationwide reckoning' with multiple fronts of fallout.

primary_source_alignment: No primary sources (court filing, roll-call, press release, official transcript) were located for this story in the dossier. CBS and ABC quote from an investigative interview transcript and panel testimony they independently obtained, but these underlying documents are not provided here for direct verification.

Because the civil complaint itself is not in the dossier, specific lawsuit allegations (e.g., the 1:42 a.m. Snapchat message, the 5:45 a.m. end time, breach-of-contract/negligence counts reported by CBS) cannot be checked against the source document and rest on single-outlet reporting.
missing_context: No primary source documents (the civil complaint, the faculty no-confidence resolution text, Hochul's executive order, or the police interview transcripts) were available in the dossier, so key specifics rest on individual outlets' characterizations.
Reuters, NYT, and NBC's Article 2 are headline-only; their framings can be described but their reporting cannot corroborate consensus facts.

The NYT framing tying the case to a 'Drop in Resolved Sexual Assault Cases Under Trump' is unverifiable from the dossier — no body text and no corroborating outlet; the national Title IX enforcement data it references is absent.

Outlets do not reconcile the apparent discrepancy over why James was appointed — whether she 'replaced' the DA (NBC) or was added as special prosecutor via Oct. 1 executive order (CBS) — nor the exact current status of the criminal probe (reopened vs. newly opening).
The accused fraternity members' side is thinly represented: NBC notes three denied allegations through attorneys, but no detailed defense account, statement, or named counsel appears across outlets.
No outlet provides the full outcome of the Ithaca Common Council vote on the proposed moratorium (CNN reports only that it was scheduled), nor the result of the faculty no-confidence resolution.

Cornell's own detailed response is only partially surfaced (CBS cites President Kotlikoff's breakdown of sanctions and a dispute over essays); a fuller official statement is not quoted across outlets.

No article explains the legal standard difference between Cornell's internal 'responsible/not responsible' finding and a criminal charging decision, which is central to understanding why expulsions occurred but no arrests did.
brief.suggested_post_type_reason: Four outlets provide full body text on the same event but with materially divergent emphases — NBC on the protest, ABC on police interview videos, CBS on the document-level factual disputes, and CNN on death threats and backlash — while three others are headline-only, including the NYT's distinctive national-politics framing. This is a coverage-report story about how the same case is being told very differently, not a single straightforward REPORT.
